summary.title: Postprocessing
summary.one_liner: You learn how to add shake, confuse and chaos postprocessing effects to a 2D OpenGL game using a multisampled framebuffer, blit, and a convolution-kernel fragment shader.
keywords: how to add screen shake in opengl
takeaways: Render the game into a multisampled framebuffer, blit it into a texture-backed framebuffer, then draw that texture onto a full-screen quad.
Use vertex shader uniforms (chaos, confuse, shake) to offset positions or texture coordinates, and the fragment shader to apply blur or edge-detection kernels.
Precompute sample offsets and convolution kernels once and pass them as uniforms instead of recalculating per fragment.
Trigger a short screen shake by setting a timer on solid collisions and disabling the effect when the timer in Update reaches zero.
summary.summary: The article is part of LearnOpenGL's 2D Breakout project and explains how to add postprocessing effects to the game. The renderer draws into a multisampled framebuffer, blits the result to a texture-backed framebuffer, and then renders that texture on a full-screen quad. A postprocessor class exposes shake, confuse and chaos flags, which are handled by a vertex shader that moves coordinates and a fragment shader that applies sampling offsets and convolution kernels. As a practical example, the shake effect is enabled for 0.05 seconds whenever the ball hits a solid block.
